W7172336769.a1.text: Critics claim simplicity reduces God to an abstract property and makes theological language vacuous.
W7172336769.a1.quote: Critics of divine simplicity argue that simplicity leads us to identify God with an abstract property and that it renders theological language semantically vacuous because divine simplicity cannot ground a plurality of true intrinsic predicates.

W7172336769.a2.text: The Thomistic doctrine of analogy keeps theological language determinate without reintroducing composition in God.
W7172336769.a2.quote: I conclude by arguing that the Thomistic doctrine of analogy does not eliminate semantic openness but renders theological language sufficiently determinate for meaning and practice, grounding meaningful God‑talk in both metaphysics and the formative practices of religious life.

W7172336769.c001.text: Critics claim that divine simplicity makes God identical to an abstract property and renders theological language vacuous because a simple God cannot ground multiple true intrinsic predicates.
W7172336769.c001.quote: Critics of divine simplicity argue that simplicity renders God identical with an abstract property and/or renders our language about God semantically vacuous since a simple God seems unable to ground a plurality of true intrinsic predicates.

W7172336769.c002.text: The paper aims to defend a broadly Thomistic account of divine simplicity against contemporary metaphysical and semantic objections.
W7172336769.c002.quote: The aim of this paper is to defend a broadly Thomistic account of divine simplicity against a cluster of contemporary metaphysical and semantic objections.

W7172336769.c003.text: The author employs modern analytic philosophy, specifically selected Fregean distinctions, to show how the criticisms of divine simplicity can be defused.
W7172336769.c003.quote: In this paper, I employ the resources of modern analytic philosophy – specifically, selected Fregean distinctions – to demonstrate how these critiques can be defused.

W7172336769.c004.text: This analogical framework supplies principled constraints on theological predication without reintroducing composition into God.
W7172336769.c004.quote: This framework supplies principled constraints on theological predication without reintroducing composition into God.

W7172336769.c005.text: The Thomistic doctrine of analogy does not eliminate semantic openness but makes theological language sufficiently determinate for meaning and practice, grounding meaningful God‑talk in metaphysics and religious practice.
W7172336769.c005.quote: I conclude by arguing that the Thomistic doctrine of analogy does not eliminate semantic openness but renders theological language sufficiently determinate for meaning and practice, grounding meaningful God‑talk in both metaphysics and the formative practices of religious life.

W7172336769.c006.text: The object‑concept distinction is far less discussed in contemporary literature on divine simplicity than the sense‑reference distinction.
W7172336769.c006.quote: The object/concept distinction, on the other hand, is far less discussed in contemporary literature on divine simplicity.

W7172336769.c007.text: Introducing the object‑concept distinction into Thomistic defenses of simplicity can illuminate the debate and constitute a genuine contribution to those defenses.
W7172336769.c007.quote: This paper argues that bringing this distinction to bear on Thomistic defences of simplicity can be illuminating and make a genuine contribution to these defences.

W7172336769.c008.text: The clarifying procedure using these distinctions, termed Fregean diagnostics, does not yet explain how theological predicates can have truth‑conditions and sufficiently determinate content.
W7172336769.c008.quote: However, the clarifying procedure involving the employment of these distinctions – Fregean diagnostics, as I’ve termed it – does not yet explain how theological predicates can have truth‑conditions and sufficiently determinate content.

W7172336769.c009.text: To address the critics’ underlying concerns, Fregean diagnostics must be located within the broader semantic‑metaphysical framework of the doctrine of analogy.
W7172336769.c009.quote: I argue that in order to address these underlying concerns of the critics of simplicity, Fregean diagnostics must be located in the broader semantic‑metaphysical framework provided by the doctrine of analogy.

W7172336769.c010.text: The analogical framework introduces a further distinction between res significata and modus significandi, providing the resources needed to ground the meaning of theological predicates.
W7172336769.c010.quote: It is this framework that introduces a crucial further distinction that Fregean diagnostics do not give us – namely, the distinction between res significata and modus significandi – and thereby provides the resources needed to ground the meaning of theological predicates.

W7172336769.c011.text: The sense‑reference distinction alone is an incomplete defensive strategy when isolated from the metaphysical framework of analogical semantics.
W7172336769.c011.quote: Thus, this paper contributes to existing debates surrounding simplicity by arguing that the more often‑used sense/reference distinction remains an incomplete defensive strategy if it is isolated from the metaphysical framework of analogical semantics.

W7172336769.c012.text: The object‑concept distinction alone also remains insufficient to ground the meaning of theological predicates.
W7172336769.c012.quote: The same goes for the more rarely used object/concept distinction: it, too, remains insufficient on its own to ground the meaning of theological predicates.

W7172336769.c013.text: The doctrine of divine simplicity denies matter–form composition, the essence–individual distinction, the essence–existence distinction, and the substance–property distinction because God has ontological priority.
W7172336769.c013.quote: More specifically, the doctrine of divine simplicity entails that the following kinds of distinctions and compositions are denied of God due to God’s ontological priority: matter–form composition, the essence–individual distinction, the essence–existence distinction, and the substance–property distinction.

W7172336769.c014.text: According to divine simplicity, God does not have properties; everything God is is all at once in one pure act.
W7172336769.c014.quote: According to the doctrine of divine simplicity, God does not have properties: everything that God is, God is all at once, in one pure act.

W7172336769.c015.text: A distinction between what God is and God’s properties would entail composition, which implies dependence and potentiality, thereby introducing a metaphysical reality prior to God.
W7172336769.c015.quote: A distinction between what God is and God’s properties would entail composition in God. Composition, in turn, implies dependence and potentiality: the whole depends on its parts and the parts could in principle be organised differently.

W7172336769.c016.text: All divine attributes have the same referent, so speaking of God’s goodness or wisdom does not pick out distinct parts in God.
W7172336769.c016.quote: Secondly, it follows that divine attributes all have the same referent: we are not picking out some distinct ‘part’ in God when we speak of God’s goodness, nor yet another when we discuss God’s wisdom.

W7172336769.c017.text: Critics present Conundrum A, concluding that because God is simple and identical with God’s goodness, goodness is God, which would identify God with an abstract property.

W7172336769.c018.text: This would indicate that God isn’t a person but a mere abstract object.
W7172336769.c018.quote: This, in turn, would indicate that God ‘isn’t a person but a mere abstract object’.

W7172336769.c019.text: Thomists hold that God is Life itself and is not a thing, nature, or abstract property, so God can act, know, and will without being a mere abstract object.
W7172336769.c019.quote: God does all these, because God is Life itself. God is not a thing, a nature, or an abstract property.

W7172336769.c020.text: Critics present Conundrum B, arguing that if God is simple, goodness and wisdom become the same thing in God, undermining the meaningfulness of multiple divine attributes.
W7172336769.c020.quote: Therefore, goodness and wisdom are the same thing in God.

W7172336769.c021.text: The doctrine of divine simplicity threatens the coherence and meaningfulness of language about God by rendering multiple divine predicates semantically vacuous.
W7172336769.c021.quote: The doctrine of divine simplicity, therefore, threatens the coherence and meaningfulness of our language about God because it makes it impossible to meaningfully predicate multiple attributes of God.

W7172336769.c022.text: Aquinas possesses a sophisticated semantic‑metaphysical apparatus, based on Fregean sense/reference distinctions, that explains how many names can be predicated of a simple God.
W7172336769.c022.quote: These allow Aquinas to explain how many names can be truly predicated of a simple God.

W7172336769.c023.text: Using Frege’s object/concept distinction we can diagnose the conundrums as semantic misreadings.
W7172336769.c023.quote: My argument is that with the help of Frege’s classic distinction between objects and concepts, we can diagnose these conundrums as semantic misreadings.

W7172336769.c024.text: Fregean distinctions are insufficient for theological predicates, so divine simplicity motivates analogical semantics as a non‑standard but determinate semantic framework.
W7172336769.c024.quote: Fregean distinctions are not sufficient to ground the meaning of theological predicates. Hence, I propose that divine simplicity motivates non-standard but sufficiently determinate semantics, namely analogical semantics.

W7172336769.c025.text: Analogical semantics supplies principled constraints on admissible divine predications, allowing ‘God is good’ while excluding ‘God is evil’ or ‘God is a chair’.
W7172336769.c025.quote: Analogical semantics also supplies principled constraints on admissible divine predications that are grounded in participation and eminence (i.e., it explains why ‘God is good’ is eligible for intrinsic predication while ‘God is evil’ or ‘God is a chair’ is not).

W7172336769.c026.text: Concepts require an object to which they apply; they are parasitic on objects.
W7172336769.c026.quote: to mean something, they need an object. Concepts require something to which they apply; they are parasitic on objects, if you like.

W7172336769.c027.text: Frege distinguishes two kinds of the verb ‘is’: the ‘is’ of predication and the ‘is’ of identification.
W7172336769.c027.quote: Following this, note also Frege’s crucial insight with regard to the word ‘is’, namely, that there are two kinds of ‘is’: the ‘is’ of predication and the ‘is’ of identification.

W7172336769.c028.text: For Aquinas, terms such as ‘goodness’ are abstract perfection terms that can be properly used of God.
W7172336769.c028.quote: Now, for Aquinas, terms such as ‘goodness’ are abstract perfection terms that can be properly used of God.

W7172336769.c029.text: Abstract names denote divine perfections but, given simplicity, they do not denote properties in God or any distinct metaphysical entities; they signify the simple divine being itself under different formal aspects.
W7172336769.c029.quote: Abstract names denote divine perfections but, given simplicity, they do not denote properties in God or any other distinct metaphysical entities. Rather, they signify the simple divine being itself, under different formal aspects.

W7172336769.c030.text: Abstract perfection terms cannot refer to distinct objects in the Fregean sense; they denote the one simple divine being only as concepts.
W7172336769.c030.quote: Abstract perfection terms, therefore, cannot refer to distinct objects in the Fregean sense but rather they denote the one, simple divine being only in the concept sense.

W7172336769.c031.text: In the statement ‘God is good’, ‘good’ is not a thing but a concept predicated of the thing we call God.
W7172336769.c031.quote: Hence, in ‘God is good’, ‘good’ is not ‘a thing’ but rather ‘good’ is a concept predicated of ‘a thing’ we call God.

W7172336769.c032.text: Conundrum A is a semantic confusion that treats ‘God is good’ as equivalent to ‘goodness is God’, mistakenly mixing object‑object with object‑concept predication.
W7172336769.c032.quote: In light of this, we can diagnose Conundrum A as the following kind of confusion: saying that [God is good = goodness is God] is like saying that [the barn is red = red is a barn]. We are confusing object–object predication with object–concept predication.

W7172336769.c033.text: Words such as goodness, divinity, simplicity, or Trinity can be used both in object and concept sense without implying that they are properties in God.
W7172336769.c033.quote: Hence, words like goodness, divinity, simplicity, or Trinity can be used both in object and concept sense, but this does not indicate a shift into the kinds of metaphysics of God, where things such as goodness are properties in God.

W7172336769.c034.text: Critics claim that statements like ‘God is goodness’ and ‘God is wisdom’ are cases of object‑object predication, analogous to ‘the evening star is the planet Venus’.
W7172336769.c034.quote: According to the critics of simplicity, ‘God is goodness’ and ‘God is wisdom’ are akin to (9): they are a case of object–object predication.

W7172336769.c035.text: The fallacy arises from failing to distinguish predication from identification; ‘good’ and ‘wise’ are concepts, not objects, so the inference that God has multiple distinct properties is mistaken.
W7172336769.c035.quote: Logically, the words ‘good’ and ‘wise’ are not objects in (4)–(7) but concepts. This, as I argued, is one of the central semantic results of the doctrine ...

W7172336769.c036.text: Using Frege’s sense‑reference distinction, ‘good’ and ‘wise’ have the same referent—the simple divine being—so multiple attributes are merely different senses of the same object, compatible with divine simplicity.
W7172336769.c036.quote: We can respond to this objection by availing ourselves of another central Fregean distinction, that between sense and reference. ‘Good’ and ‘wise’ both have the same referent: the simple, undivided divine being.

W7172336769.c037.text: The traditional doctrine of divine simplicity denies that God possesses any properties; it does not identify God with properties.
W7172336769.c037.quote: the traditional doctrine of simplicity does not identify God with God’s properties – rather, it denies that God has any properties at all.

W7172336769.c038.text: How can theological predicates have sufficiently determinate content and truth‑conditions if the Fregean distinction alone does not provide a theory of their meaning?
W7172336769.c038.quote: the Fregean distinction does not yet explain how theological predicates can have sufficiently determinate content and truth-conditions.

W7172336769.c039.text: All attempts to ground content without sacrificing divine simplicity, such as minimal truth‑makers, trope theory, property exemplification, and divine attributes as determinables of a super‑property, fail.
W7172336769.c039.quote: all attempts to ground content without sacrificing simplicity (such as minimal truth‑makers, trope theory, property exemplification, divine attributes as determinables of a super‑property) fail.

W7172336769.c040.text: The doctrine of analogy can ground the meaningfulness of theological language without implying any composition in God.
W7172336769.c040.quote: I’ll demonstrate how the doctrine of analogy can ground the meaning­fulness of theological language without implying composition in God.

W7172336769.c041.text: Answering worries about semantic vacuity requires embedding Fregean diagnostics in a broader metaphysical framework, for example analogy.
W7172336769.c041.quote: Answering these worries about meaning requires turning from semantics to metaphysics: Fregean diagnostics must be embedded in a broader metaphysical framework, e.g. analogy.

W7172336769.c042.text: The Thomistic doctrine of analogy can provide principled constraints and sufficiently determinate content for divine predicates, thereby answering residual worries about meaning.
W7172336769.c042.quote: Our aim in this section is not to rehearse a generic version of the Thomistic doctrine of analogy but to demonstrate how this doctrine can answer the residual worries about meaning from Section 3 by providing principled constraints and sufficiently determinate content for divine predicates.

W7172336769.c043.text: Frege’s distinction between concepts and objects offers a genuine contribution to a Thomistic defence of divine simplicity.
W7172336769.c043.quote: Frege does have something genuinely interesting to contribute to a Thomistic defence of simplicity, namely, his distinction between concepts and objects.

W7172336769.c044.text: Aquinas lacks a Frege‑like sharp logical distinction between complete referential expressions and unsaturated predicative expressions.
W7172336769.c044.quote: Aquinas does, of course, make a distinction between that of which something is predicated and what is being predicated, but he does not quite have a Frege‑like sharp logical distinction between complete referential expressions and unsaturated predicative expressions.

W7172336769.c045.text: The concept/object strategy remains incomplete because it cannot fully address residual worries about the content of theological predicates.
W7172336769.c045.quote: this strategy, like the sense/reference strategy, remains incomplete because it cannot fully address residual worries about the content of theological predicates.

W7172336769.c046.text: To address those worries we must employ Aquinas’s distinction between what is signified (res significata) and the mode of signification (modus significandi).
W7172336769.c046.quote: we must bring in a further distinction from Aquinas that Frege does not have, namely the distinction between what is signified (res significata) and the mode of signification (modus significandi).

W7172336769.c047.text: In God the mode of signifying is creaturely, but what is signified is truly found in God and does not entail any kind of composition.
W7172336769.c047.quote: God, the mode of signifying is creaturely (i.e., speaking of goodness as a property that inheres in an entity), but what is signified (res significata) is truly found in God, except in a metaphysical mode that we cannot properly conceive. We can only say negatively that this mode is not such that it entails any kind of composition.

W7172336769.c048.text: Analogy’s principle holds that creaturely predication, suited to a world of multiplicity, can only speak of God in a creaturely mode, with plurality residing in the mode of signifying, not the signified reality.
W7172336769.c048.quote: Here is also where analogy, in its semantic dimension, finds its originating principle: for creaturely predication is made for a world such as ours – a world of multiplicity and difference – and can, therefore, only speak of God in a creaturely mode. ‘Good’ and ‘wise’ are distinct concepts because our intellect abstracts different aspects from creaturely perfections; in God, there are not distinct aspects but one act.

W7172336769.c049.text: Critics argue that analogy obscures the meaning of terms applied to God because we cannot know whether divine goodness entails the same as human goodness.
W7172336769.c049.quote: analogy obscures the meaning of terms when applied to God: human goodness might, for example, mean that one does not needlessly cause the innocent to suffer, but we have no way of knowing if divine goodness entails the same.

W7172336769.c050.text: Defenders of analogy reply that divine attributes are not entirely senseless; we simply do not know the particular sense in which they obtain in God.
W7172336769.c050.quote: the defenders of analogy would respond to this by arguing that attributes such as ‘love’ are not entirely senseless when applied to God; we just do not know ‘the particular sense in which God’s love, power, or goodness obtain’ with respect to God.

W7172336769.c051.text: The author replies that Misiewicz errs by assuming defenders of analogy cannot specify what makes language about God intelligible.
W7172336769.c051.quote: the thing that leads Misiewicz astray is thinking that the defenders of analogy have no way of specifying what this something is.

W7172336769.c052.text: Much of the confusion about divine simplicity arises from failing to appreciate its apophatic character.
W7172336769.c052.quote: much of the confusion here lies in not appreciating the apophatic character of the classical doctrine of simplicity.

W7172336769.c053.text: Making the relational comparison between creaturely and divine goodness requires putting God in a genus.
W7172336769.c053.quote: Misiewicz says (ibid., pp. 56–60) that making this relational comparison requires putting God in a genus.

W7172336769.c054.text: The reason some think the difference in analogy is unspecified is that they treat the semantic dimension of analogy in isolation from its metaphysical background.
W7172336769.c054.quote: I reckon that the reason Misiewicz, Williams and others think of the difference in analogy as unspecified – a semantic can of worms that opens up the possibility of anything goes predication – is that they treat the semantic dimension of analogy in isolationfromitsmetaphysicalbackground.

W7172336769.c055.text: Analogy is a semantic thesis grounded in the primary metaphysical thesis that creatures participate in perfections pre‑contained in God.
W7172336769.c055.quote: They miss the fact that an analogy is a semantic thesis that is grounded in a primary metaphysical thesis: creatures participate in perfections pre-contained in God.

W7172336769.c056.text: The intelligibility of theological language is grounded because God, as creator, causes all things to reflect Him.
W7172336769.c056.quote: This is the something that grounds the intelligibility of theological language: because God is the creator of all things, all things – to the degree that they have being – reflect God.

W7172336769.c057.text: A fixed metaphysical relation between God and creatures grounds the meaning of analogical predicates and stops semantic regress.
W7172336769.c057.quote: This also puts a stop to the kind of semantic regress Williams worries about: there is a fixed metaphysical relation between God and creatures that grounds the meaning of analogical predicates.

W7172336769.c058.text: Individual entities are not analogies of God; rather, being itself is analogical.
W7172336769.c058.quote: In fact, strictly speaking, it is not the case that individual entities are analogies of God.

W7172336769.c059.text: There can be no analogy between any creaturely entity and a simple God because abstraction by confusion contradicts simplicity.
W7172336769.c059.quote: Thus, there can be no analogy between some creaturely entity X and a simple God.

W7172336769.c060.text: The proportional unity involved in analogy is metaphysical, not arithmetic, and is sui generis because God does not belong to any genus.
W7172336769.c060.quote: the proportional unity is not an arithmetic one but rather a metaphysical one, stemming from God’s causal relationship to creation. It is therefore a sui generis relation – indeed, it is a sui generis relation precisely because God does not belong in any genus.

W7172336769.c061.text: Analogical predication presupposes composition in concepts but not in God; the lack of composition in God makes the predication analogical.
W7172336769.c061.quote: the concepts – and, therefore, analogical predication – presupposes composition, but this does not mean that composition must be read into God in Godself. In fact, it is precisely because there is no composition in God that the predication in question is analogical.

W7172336769.c062.text: For Aquinas, analogy is not merely about causality; God is essentially Good, not just the cause of goodness.
W7172336769.c062.quote: Analogy – for Aquinas, anyways – is not simply a matter of causality.

W7172336769.c063.text: Through analogical reasoning we can know that God would never needlessly cause innocent suffering.
W7172336769.c063.quote: We can therefore know, through analogical reasoning, that God’s goodness means that God would never needlessly cause the innocent to suffer.

W7172336769.c064.text: Only pure perfections can be predicated of God analogically; predicates like ‘God is a chair’ or ‘God can do evil’ are incoherent.
W7172336769.c064.quote: only predicates that signify pure perfections – such as goodness, wisdom, knowledge, being, and life – can be predicated of God analogically since such perfections exist in God eminently and without limitation. By contrast, ‘God is a chair’ involves a category mistake because being a chair entails a material mode of being that God does not have.

W7172336769.c065.text: If God is simple and does not exemplify any property, then all predication about God lacks a subject that makes propositions true.
W7172336769.c065.quote: there is the objection that all predication requires a subject who exemplifies a property. If God is simple and, therefore, does not exemplify a property, then we have no way of predicating anything of God and no way of knowing what is the truth-value of any proposition p in the form of ‘God is X’ because we do not know what in God renders p true.

W7172336769.c066.text: Adopting a truth‑maker view solves the problem: God Himself is the truth‑maker for divine predicates without needing property exemplification.
W7172336769.c066.quote: From the perspective of the truthmaker theory of predication, there is nothing problematic about saying that God is identical with his nature, goodness, power, wisdom, or any other such things.

W7172336769.c067.text: Taking divine simplicity seriously implies that viewing God as an exception to usual truth‑maker functions is expected, not ad hoc.
W7172336769.c067.quote: if we begin from taking divine simplicity seriously, then adopting the view that God provides an exception case for how truth-makers usually function is not adhoc – it is just what we would expect to follow from God’s ontological uniqueness.

W7172336769.c068.text: The objection assumes that every true predication must be classificatory, locating its subject within a genus by attributing an intrinsic feature.
W7172336769.c068.quote: The key mistake in this objection is the assumption that every true predication must be classificatory – i.e., it must locate its subject within a genus by attributing it an intrinsic feature.

W7172336769.c069.text: The concern can be answered by distinguishing intrinsic perfection predication, extrinsic denominations, and metatheoretical role descriptions.
W7172336769.c069.quote: We can answer this concern by distinguishing between intrinsic perfection predication, extrinsic denominations, and metatheoretical role descriptions.

W7172336769.c070.text: Intrinsic perfection predication (e.g., God is good, wise, simple) states what God is in Godself, namely God’s simple essence.
W7172336769.c070.quote: Analogical predication applies to the first of these because intrinsic perfection predication (God is ‘good’, ‘wise’, ‘simple’) involves statements about what God is in Godself – God’s simple essence.

W7172336769.c071.text: Calling God the source of creaturely perfections expresses a metaphysical dependence relation, not an added intrinsic perfection.
W7172336769.c071.quote: To characterise God as the source of creaturely perfections, however, is not to add an additional perfection to God and thereby characterised God’s simple essence as such – it is to simply characterise a metaphysical dependence relation between God and creatures.

W7172336769.c072.text: Saying ‘God is good’ is true because God’s being metaphysically grounds the proposition’s truth, not because it adds an intrinsic predicate.
W7172336769.c072.quote: Similarly, on a truth-maker approach: to say that ‘God is good’ is true is to say that God’s very being is sufficient for (and thus metaphysically grounds) the truth of the proposition.

W7172336769.c073.text: Speaking of God as ‘the truth‑maker of p’ is a metatheoretical role description, not a classificatory predicate.
W7172336769.c073.quote: Thus, to speak of God as ‘the truth-maker of p’ is to speak of God in terms of metatheoretical role descriptions.

W7172336769.c074.text: Critics ask what it actually means to say that God is good.
W7172336769.c074.quote: What, they might ask, does it actually mean to say that God is good?

W7172336769.c075.text: The objection presents a false dichotomy: either a theory fixes theological meanings determinately or it renders them vacuous.
W7172336769.c075.quote: My main issue with this objection is that it involves a false dichotomy: a theological theory of meaning must either be able to provide the semantic tools for determinately fixing the meaning of theological predicates or accept that theological predicates are semantically vacuous.

W7172336769.c076.text: No theological theory can determinately fix meanings because our understanding of predicates like ‘good’ applied to God is always incomplete.
W7172336769.c076.quote: I would like to suggest, however, that it is unlikely that any theological theory of meaning can determinately fix the meaning of theological predicates because our understanding of the meaning of such predicates as ‘good’ when applied to God is always incomplete.

W7172336769.c077.text: A better standard for a theological theory of meaning is to provide grounding for theological meanings that are sufficiently determinate.
W7172336769.c077.quote: Therefore, in my view, a better standard of success for a theological theory of meaning is that our theory should provide theoretical grounding for thinking of theological meanings as sufficiently determinate.

W7172336769.c078.text: The Thomistic doctrine of analogy can meet the standard of providing sufficiently determinate theological meanings.
W7172336769.c078.quote: I think that the Thomistic doctrine of analogy can meet this standard.

W7172336769.c079.text: Divine simplicity does not make theological language vacuous; it requires a disciplined, analogical mode of predication grounded in participatory metaphysics.
W7172336769.c079.quote: The central claim of this paper, then, has been that divine simplicity does not render theological language vacuous, but instead requires a disciplined, analogical mode of predication grounded in participatory metaphysics.

W7172336769.c080.text: Analogy is a metaphysical doctrine that grounds religious sense‑making practices and cannot be reduced to logical principles.
W7172336769.c080.quote: Analogy ... is a metaphysical doctrine that grounds certain religious practices of sense-making and language-use that cannot be reduced to logical principles.

objections.text: Consider two theologians, Ana and Ben, who both accept the Thomistic analogy framework and apply it to 'God is wise.' Ana reads res significata 'wisdom' as analogically proportioned, so the predicate has a determinate content: God's wisdom exceeds creaturely wisdom while sharing its ratio. Ben uses the same framework but treats the modus significandi as fixing that God's wisdom is identical with God's essence, yielding that 'wise' applies with a content Ana would call empty. Both pass the framework's constraints: 'God is good' is admitted, 'God is evil' and 'God is a chair' are excluded. Yet asked whether God knows future contingents, Ana answers yes in a sense that entails divine foreknowledge constrains human freedom, while Ben answers yes in a sense that does not. The framework's constraints are satisfied by both, and the predicate's content is determinate for each speaker, but the content differs and no analogical rule selects between them. The determinacy supplied is local to each reading, not shared, so it cannot ground a common practice of God-talk.
objections.premise_fails_because: c042 fails because analogical constraints exclude only gross misapplications (chair, evil) and do not fix a single determinate content for divine predicates, so the claimed determinacy is not sufficient to answer the worries about shared meaning and practice.

objections.text: The premise assumes that drawing a line between res significata and modus significandi automatically yields the semantic resources to ground theological predicates. But this is a formal distinction about how language operates, not a substantive account of what the divine res significata contains. Consider the predicate 'good': the distinction tells us that the mode of signifying is creaturely, and that God is the thing signified. It gives us no purchase on what God's goodness consists in; it merely labels the gap between human concept and divine reality. The analogical framework denies that the modus applies to God, and the res in its divine mode remains unknown, so the distinction leaves the content of 'good' as applied to God semantically underdetermined. The inference from introducing this distinction to providing resources to ground meaning therefore misses a step: classifying the structure of signification is not the same as determining its content. The premise treats a map of semantic relations as if it were the territory of semantic determination.
objections.premise_fails_because: Premise W7172336769.c010 fails because it conflates the formal classification of signification-structure with the substantive grounding of predicate-meaning, leaving the content of divine predicates unexplained.

objections.text: Consider a critic who argues that divine simplicity is incoherent because 'God is wise' and 'God is good' seem to predicate distinct attributes of one simple being. A defender responds using only Frege's sense/reference distinction: both sentences share the same reference (God himself) while differing in sense, much as 'the morning star is bright' and 'the evening star is bright' differ in sense but co-refer. This directly defuses the critic's worry that distinct predicates imply distinct properties in God. The response is complete without invoking analogy, proportionality, or any analogical framework. The critic's concern—that simplicity threatens coherent predication—is addressed purely by the Fregean diagnostic that sameness of reference is compatible with difference of sense. The premise claims Fregean diagnostics MUST be located within the doctrine of analogy to address such concerns, but this case shows the concerns are already addressable without that framework.
objections.premise_fails_because: Premise W7172336769.c009 fails because Fregean sense/reference diagnostics can independently resolve the critic's worry about distinct predicates implying distinct divine properties, making the 'must' claim false.

objections.text: In the practice of ritual chant, the phrase 'God is a lion' is both meaningful and liturgical, yet it violates the proposed constraints by equating the divine with a creature. The chant assumes a symbolic, not literal, mode where predications derive their force from communal usage and mythic resonance rather than semantic exclusivity. Here, the framework fails to account for how non-literal, culturally embedded language can carry theological weight without collapsing into absurdity or contradiction. The constraints, if applied, would dismiss valid devotional expressions merely for defying analytic neatness.
objections.premise_fails_because: W7172336769.c025 fails because it cannot accommodate meaningful non-literal predications like 'God is a lion' that function in religious practice.

objections.text: C003 claims that selected Fregean distinctions can defuse criticisms of divine simplicity. It smuggles in the assumption that the sense/reference distinction is a neutral, self-sufficient diagnostic: pick it out, apply it, and the criticism dissolves. But the Fregean distinction is not neutral. Its operation presupposes a determinate referent—God as a single, unified object to which multiple senses attach. The criticism of divine simplicity targets exactly that presupposition: if God is simple, it is unclear whether 'good' and 'wise' pick out one referent or whether the predicates carve God into incompatible slices. The Fregean move can only 'defuse' the criticism if it already grants the unity the critic denies. C009 and C010 confirm this: the Fregean distinctions cannot stand alone; they require embedding in the analogical framework (res significata / modus significandi) to secure a determinate referent. So the Fregean distinctions do not defuse the criticism; the analogical framework does, and the Fregean layer is merely a local diagnostic that functions only because the framework has already supplied the unity. C003 needs the Fregean distinctions to be self-sufficient but cannot have them, because their very operation presupposes the unified referent the criticism challenges.
objections.premise_fails_because: W7172336769.c003 fails because it treats the Fregean sense/reference distinction as a neutral, self-sufficient diagnostic, when in fact the distinction's operation presupposes a determinate unified referent—the very unity the criticism of divine simplicity denies—so the Fregean layer cannot defuse the criticism without already importing the answer the analogical framework must supply.

objections.text: Consider a theologian, Emma, who uses the Thomistic doctrine of analogy to interpret divine predicates. She believes that 'God is good' has a determinate meaning, but her interpretation relies on a complex web of metaphysical assumptions. In practice, Emma's community has varying understandings of 'good', leading to disagreements about God's nature. Despite the doctrine's constraints, the community's diverse perspectives on divine goodness persist, indicating that determinacy in theological language is not solely due to the doctrine's supplies.
objections.premise_fails_because: The hidden premise fails because it assumes that the determinacy supplied by the Thomistic doctrine of analogy is sufficient to answer worries about meaning, when in fact, the complexities of human interpretation and the persistence of diverse perspectives can undermine such determinacy.

objections.text: Consider the monk Ioannis of a remote monastery. He receives the uncreated divine energies in the Divine Liturgy, experiencing God’s love, wisdom, and power as living realities, not as merely semantic predicates. A philosopher using the analogical framework would say the rule “allow ‘God is good’ but exclude ‘God is a chair’” secures meaning. Yet Ioannis knows that calling God a chair is barred because the divine energies cannot be reduced to any created category, not because of a linguistic constraint. The same reason that permits “God is love” is the participation in the uncreated energy of love, which transcends any analogical semantic scheme. Thus the premise that analogical semantics alone supplies the principled exclusion fails to account for the essence‑energies distinction that truly governs divine predication.
objections.premise_fails_because: Premise W7172336769.c025 fails because analogical semantics alone cannot determine admissible divine predications; the true constraints come from the Eastern Orthodox distinction between God's essence and uncreated energies.

objections.text: A theologian believes that because analogy provides "sufficiently determinate content," the predicate "wise" and the predicate "good" correspond to distinct, determinate metaphysical specifications within the divine essence. Consequently, they treat God as a composite of these distinct specifications. This view forces a composition upon God, transforming the single, undivided Act of Being into a collection of distinct, determinate properties. By attempting to secure semantic determinacy, the theologian inadvertently destroys divine simplicity, which requires that God be absolutely without parts or multiplicity.
objections.premise_fails_because: W7172336769.c042 fails because "sufficiently determinate content" implies a multiplicity of distinct metaphysical specifications that would violate the principle of divine simplicity.

objections.text: A semantic theorist argues that for a predicate to carry determinate content, there must be a fixed and exhaustive relationship between the signifier and the signified. The doctrine of analogy, by design, preserves 'semantic openness,' meaning the relationship between the human term and the divine reality is intentionally left under-specified. If this relationship is under-specified, the 'content' provided by analogy consists only of negative constraints—limiting what the term cannot mean—without providing the positive, specific information required for determinacy. Consequently, the openness that the argument seeks to preserve prevents the term from actually possessing the determinate content necessary for meaningful predication.
objections.premise_fails_because: W7172336769.c042 fails because semantic openness and sufficiently determinate content are mutually exclusive.

objections.text: Imagine a theological community that uses only Fregean sense-reference analysis to govern divine predicates, with no recourse to analogy or the res significata/modus significandi distinction. They apply a compositional test: a sense of a predicate is admissible for God iff it can be coherently attributed to a being possessing maximal perfection, where coherence is checked via Fregean criteria (no internal contradiction in the sense, compatibility with other admissible senses). For 'good,' they distinguish the sense 'morally excellent in finite agents' from 'infinite source of all perfections'; the first is excluded (it implies limitation), the second admitted. For 'evil,' every candidate sense contradicts maximal perfection, so all are excluded. For 'chair,' the sense entails spatial extension and material composition, incompatible with the admissible sense of 'divine,' so excluded. The community achieves fully determinate, principled constraints on divine predications—knowing which senses are admissible—using Fregean diagnostics alone. Determinacy here is supplied by sense analysis and perfection-coherence testing, not by any analogical framework.
objections.premise_fails_because: Premise W7172336769.arg1.r1 fails because Fregean diagnostics alone can supply determinate admissibility constraints on divine predicates, so the analogical framework is not the sole supplier of determinacy.

objections.text: Two trained Thomistic theologians, A and B, both accept the analogical framework and its fixed metaphysical relation between creatures and God. A argues 'God is mutable' is inadmissible: mutability belongs to creatures as material composites, and the metaphysical relation traces only perfections to God. B argues 'God is mutable' is admissible: creaturely mutability includes responsiveness to love, a perfection rooted in divine goodness, so the analogical relation permits the predication when understood analogically. Both invoke the same fixed metaphysical relation to creatures. The framework provides no principled mechanism to settle whether mutability traces to material potency (excluded) or to responsive goodness (included). Thus the fixed metaphysical relation fails to supply constraints sufficient to exclude 'God is mutable'—a predication classical theism must reject. The framework's exclusion power depends on prior, independent judgments about which creaturely features count as perfections—judgments the framework itself does not generate.
objections.premise_fails_because: Premise W7172336769.arg1.r2 fails because the Thomistic analogical framework's fixed metaphysical relation to creatures does not by itself yield principled constraints sufficient to exclude ill-formed divine predications, as shown by the case where two theologians invoking the same framework reach opposite conclusions about the admissibility of 'God is mutable.'

objections.text: r3 concedes that the analogical framework excludes ill-formed predications (e.g., 'God is a chair') only conditional on a prior, independent classification of pure perfections. The argument needs r3 to function as a modest concession: the framework cannot settle every contested case ('God is mutable'), yet still supplies the determinacy that makes God-talk meaningful. But r3 severs the very link the conclusion requires. If even the exclusion of plainly incoherent predications depends on an external classification the framework does not itself generate, then the framework contributes no determinacy at all. The 'sufficiently determinate for meaning and practice' work attributed to the Thomistic doctrine in c005 is actually performed by the prior classification of creaturely features as pure perfections. r3 is treated as a limitation on scope (the framework cannot settle hard cases) while silently shifting the source of all determinacy outside the framework. The premise thus fails to support mp: it shows the framework is parasitic on an external input, not that it supplies principled constraints while leaving residual openness.
objections.premise_fails_because: W7172336769.arg1.r3 fails because it relocates the source of all determinacy to an external classification of pure perfections, leaving the analogical framework itself contributing no principled constraints, which is precisely what the conclusion requires it to supply.

restatements.paper_vocabulary: Analogical determinacy is local, not shared: two speakers who both adopt the Thomistic framework, with its res significata/modus significandi distinction, can fix divine predicates such as 'God is wise' to incompatible contents (ratio-preserving analogy versus identity of wisdom with essence), and the framework's admissibility constraints, which exclude 'God is evil' and 'God is a chair', do not select between them on the question of divine foreknowledge and creaturely freedom, so the content supplied cannot ground a common practice of God-talk.
restatements.plain_english: Two people can follow the same rules for talking about God and still mean different things by the same word. One takes 'God is wise' to mean God has a wisdom like ours but far greater, and the other takes it to mean God's wisdom is just God's own nature. The rules rule out nonsense like 'God is a chair,' but they do not decide between these two meanings. So when they disagree about whether God knows the future in a way that affects our freedom, the rules do not settle who is right, and the meaning each one has is their own, not one they share.
restatements.neighboring_tradition: This is a shared-language or public-meaning objection of the kind raised in the epistemology of disagreement and in debates over semantic underdetermination: a rule set can screen out clearly false predications and still leave a term's content fixed differently across speakers who all comply, so that no common community standard of correct use is secured. It parallels the worry that a shared framework yields private rather than public meaning, and the point that admissibility constraints are necessary but not sufficient for a shared, practice-sustaining semantics.

restatements.paper_vocabulary: The objection contends that the proposed analogical constraints on admissible divine predications, which license 'God is good' and exclude 'God is evil' or 'God is a chair,' are too rigid: 'God is a lion' is meaningful and liturgically functional in ritual chant, yet it breaches the constraints by assimilating the divine to a creature. On this view, the chant operates in a symbolic rather than literal mode, drawing its theological force from communal usage and mythic resonance rather than from the semantic exclusivity the analogical framework requires, so the constraints wrongly screen out valid devotional predication merely because it resists analytic neatness.
restatements.plain_english: The rules that are supposed to decide which things can be said about God are too strict. People in religious singing say 'God is a lion' and it means something real and helps their worship, even though it seems to make God like an animal. The chant works as a picture, not a literal claim, and gets its meaning from how the community uses it and from its old stories. So the rules throw out good religious speech just because it doesn't fit neatly into logic.
restatements.neighboring_tradition: In the philosophy of religious language and liturgical hermeneutics, this is the familiar complaint that a regulative grammar of religious predication, here a constraint-based account of divine predicates, overlooks the performative, metaphorical, and symbolic functions of worship, so that it misclassifies devotional idiom such as ritual chant or mythic imagery as category error or contradiction. Its counterpart is the claim that meaning in religious speech is fixed by communal practice and symbolic resonance rather than by literal semantic exclusion, as in the Wittgensteinian and Lindbeckian treatments of religious language as grammar and practice.

rounds.content: Not a misreading: The objection directly attacks the necessity claim in W7172336769.c009 — that Fregean diagnostics MUST be located within the doctrine of analogy to address critics' concerns — by presenting a case where Frege's sense/reference distinction alone defuses a specific worry about divine simplicity. rounds.speaker: defender_a
rounds.content: You are right that sense/reference does real work against the narrow charge: if 'God is wise' and 'God is good' co-refer to the simple being, distinct predicates need not mean distinct properties in God, and the paper itself grants this at [W7172336769.c036]. But your case establishes only that the coherence of multiple predication survives. The critics' underlying concern, as the argument frames it, is whether such predicates have determinate content at all, and Frege's distinction does not supply that. A sense is a mode of presentation, so 'God is good' and 'God is wise' can differ in sense, yet nothing in the sense/reference pair tells us which senses are admissible for God and which ("God is a chair", "God is evil") are excluded. Your own morning-star example works only because both senses are already fixed by ordinary, determinate use. For divine predicates that use is absent, and the paper's concession at [W7172336769.c050], that we do not know the particular sense in which attributes obtain in God, marks exactly the gap. Your reply therefore answers the identity worry and leaves the determinacy worry open. The argument's stronger claim, that Fregean diagnostics must be located within analogy, overreaches: it is correct only if the determinacy worry is among the critics' concerns, and I hold that it is. I concede that c009 as worded says 'must' where the defensible claim is 'must, for the determinacy concern', and I would restate it that way.
rounds.revised_premise: Fregean sense/reference suffices to rebut the charge that distinct predicates imply distinct properties in God, but the further concern about determinate content for divine predicates requires the analogical framework, so Fregean diagnostics must be located within analogy only with respect to that determinacy concern.

rounds.speaker: attacker
rounds.content: You concede that c009's "must" overreaches as worded, and I welcome that. But your restated claim still falters. You say Fregean diagnostics must be located within analogy *for the determinacy concern*. Yet your own reply shows the Fregean machinery does independent work: it resolves the identity worry standalone, and you admit this. The determinacy worry, if genuine, is a separate concern that analogy addresses on its own terms—per c025 and c042, analogy supplies admissibility constraints. But that means analogy is a *supplement* to the Fregean tools, not a *framework within which they must be located*. The subordination c009 asserts is the wrong structural relationship. Fregean diagnostics and analogical semantics handle different worries side by side; the former need not be embedded in the latter. So even your restated "must, for the determinacy concern" wrongly frames supplementation as subordination. c009 should say Fregean diagnostics are *insufficient without* analogy, not that they must be *located within* it.

rounds.speaker: defender_a
rounds.content:
You are right that the rejoinder exposes a real problem: 'located within' is the wrong relation if the Fregean tools do independent work on the identity worry. But I resist the reading that analogy is merely a side-supplement. The paper's own concession at [W7172336769.c050], that we do not know the particular sense in which divine attributes obtain, shows that the Fregean distinction presupposes determinate senses it cannot itself supply. Sense/reference tells us that 'good' and 'wise' can present one referent differently; it does not tell us which senses are admissible for God, and [W3115675310.c042] rightly notes that Fregean sense does not by itself support simplicity. So the dependence runs one way: the Fregean diagnostic handles non-identity of predicates, while the admissibility of the senses it distinguishes is fixed by the analogical framework, which is what c025 and c042 claim. Where I concede: 'must be located within' is too strong as a description of the whole relationship, since the identity worry is answered without analogy. The defensible claim is that Fregean diagnostics are insufficient for the determinacy concern without analogical constraints, which is the 'insufficient without' wording you proposed. That weakens c009 from structural subordination to a conditional dependence, and the conclusion c005 survives only if the determinacy concern is among the critics' central worries, which the paper's own framing of 'residual worries about meaning' supports.

rounds.speaker: defender_a
rounds.content:
You are right that the distinction by itself is formal, and c010 read in isolation overclaims. But the argument never asks the distinction to tell us what God's goodness consists in. Its claim is that the analogical framework supplies constraints and a fixed relation to creatures: 'good' is admitted of God because the res signified (perfection) is truly in God while the modus is creaturely [W7172336769.c047], and this is what excludes 'God is a chair' and 'God is evil' [W7172336769.c025]. Determinacy here means determinacy of admissibility and of truth-conditions relative to a grounding relation, not a positive inventory of divine goodness. That is the sense in which the Thomistic framework is said to stop semantic regress [W7172336769.c057]. Your strongest point is the open question that the paper itself flags: without a theory of content, truth-conditions remain unsettled [W7172336769.c038]. I accept that the bare res/modus distinction does not carry that load, and that the premise as written leans on it too heavily. The Scotist-Thomist dispute over whether attributes are literally or analogically predicated shows how contested this is [W2521362363.a2], and the worry that analogy is of doubtful validity remains live [W2912734992.a3]. The argument survives only if its determinacy claim is restricted to constraint and admissibility, and the conclusion is weakened to match.

rounds.content: Not a misreading: The objection directly attacks the claim in r2 that the analogical framework supplies 'principled admissibility constraints and a fixed metaphysical relation to creatures sufficient to exclude ill-formed divine predications.' It argues that the framework cannot settle whether 'God is mutable' is admissible or inadmissible, since both sides invoke the same fixed metaphysical relation but reach opposite conclusions depending on prior judgments about which creaturely features count as perfections. This challenges the sufficiency of the framework's exclusion power, which is exactly what r2 asserts. The objection does not misread the premise; it attacks the premise as stated.

rounds.speaker: defender_a
rounds.content:
Your objection targets the step from 'the framework excludes ill-formed predications' to 'the framework excludes God is mutable.' The argument's r2 premise is narrower: the framework supplies admissibility constraints, and it grants that positive content of predicates like 'good' is not fixed by the framework. Your case is that A and B both invoke the same relation yet reach opposite verdicts on 'mutable,' so the relation fails to discriminate. I grant the datum: shared premises do not settle a contested classification. But the framework's constraint is not a decision procedure; it says the predicate must trace to a pure perfection, and it is the metaphysics of creaturely perfection, not the semantics, that decides which features count. [W7172336769.c064] already requires that only pure perfections be predicated analogically, so 'mutable' is admissible only if mutability as such is a pure perfection. A's reading treats mutability as material potency, which is a defect and so not a perfection, and that is the mainstream classical verdict. B must argue that responsiveness to love is a distinct perfection that is separable from potency, and that is a substantive claim the framework does not make. So the disagreement shows the framework is incomplete at the margins, not that it lacks exclusion power. I concede the stronger reading of r2: the framework's exclusion power depends on prior judgments about perfections, as the objection says. The argument as stated claims determinacy 'for meaning and practice,' and that claim does not survive unless it is qualified to say the framework constrains predication without settling contested perfection-classifications. The revised premise is that the Thomistic framework supplies admissibility constraints conditional on an independent, prior classification of pure perfections.

rounds.content:
You are right that the argument's own revised premise (r2) concedes that analogy does not by itself fix the positive content of 'good', so your negative-constraints point lands on that part of the claim. But you read 'determinate' as requiring an exhaustive relation, and the argument does not need that. The determinacy it claims is the determinacy needed to exclude ill-formed predications ('God is a chair', 'God is evil') and to ground a fixed relation to creatures [W7172336769.c025, W7172336769.c057], and that is a positive, if partial, specification: a term applies to God in virtue of a perfection pre-contained in God and participated in by creatures [W7172336769.c055]. Admissibility is itself informative about which senses are available. Openness, on the argument's own account, concerns the manner of signification (modus significandi) rather than the thing signified (res significata) [W7172336769.c010], so the under-specification you identify is at the level of how the term signifies, not whether it signifies anything determinate. Your strongest remaining point is the open question that the argument has not answered: how truth-conditions are fixed without a theory of meaning [W7172336769.c038]. I think the argument survives the objection as scoped to admissibility and practical meaning, but not as a claim of full semantic determinacy for positive predicates, and I concede that narrowing.

The doctrine of analogy distinguishes the res significata from the modus significandi [W7172336769.c010]: what we signify—goodness itself—is positively affirmed of God, while only the creaturely mode of signification is left open. This positive content is grounded in the fixed metaphysical relation that creatures participate in perfections pre-contained in God [W7172336769.c055], which anchors the meaning of analogical predicates and stops semantic regress [W7172336769.c057]. Consequently, 'God is good' carries determinate truth-conditions—we know God is the eminent source of goodness and not evil—without our comprehension being exhaustive [W7172336769.c005, W7172336769.a2]. Your requirement that determinacy demands a fixed and exhaustive mapping conflates sufficient determinacy for meaning and practice with total semantic closure, a standard the argument never accepts and does not need.

rounds.content: You concede that the *modus significandi* is left open, yet you claim this doesn't undermine determinacy. This is a contradiction regarding semantic content. The content of a predicate in a specific sentence—"God is good"—is not merely the *res significata* (goodness) in isolation; it is the specification of how that *res* applies to the subject. If the *modus* is intentionally under-specified to maintain openness, then the truth-conditions for the predication remain under-specified. Knowing that God is the "eminent source" of goodness is a generic metaphysical claim, but it fails to provide the determinate content required to distinguish *how* God is good from any other indeterminate way of being a "source." You have preserved the *object* of the sign, but you have failed to provide a determinate *meaning* for the specific application of that sign to God.

naive_questioner.question: If the words we use for God are kept "open" and not fully defined, how can they still be clear enough to actually mean something specific?

objection.text: Consider two theologians, Ana and Ben, who both accept the Thomistic analogy framework and apply it to 'God is wise.' Ana reads res significata 'wisdom' as analogically proportioned, so the predicate has a determinate content: God's wisdom exceeds creaturely wisdom while sharing its ratio. Ben uses the same framework but treats the modus significandi as fixing that God's wisdom is identical with God's essence, yielding that 'wise' applies with a content Ana would call empty. Both pass the framework's constraints: 'God is good' is admitted, 'God is evil' and 'God is a chair' are excluded. Yet asked whether God knows future contingents, Ana answers yes in a sense that entails divine foreknowledge constrains human freedom, while Ben answers yes in a sense that does not. The framework's constraints are satisfied by both, and the predicate's content is determinate for each speaker, but the content differs and no analogical rule selects between them. The determinacy supplied is local to each reading, not shared, so it cannot ground a common practice of God-talk.
objection.premise_fails_because: c042 fails because analogical constraints exclude only gross misapplications (chair, evil) and do not fix a single determinate content for divine predicates, so the claimed determinacy is not sufficient to answer the worries about shared meaning and practice.

objection.text: The premise assumes that drawing a line between res significata and modus significandi automatically yields the semantic resources to ground theological predicates. But this is a formal distinction about how language operates, not a substantive account of what the divine res significata contains. Consider the predicate 'good': the distinction tells us that the mode of signifying is creaturely, and that God is the thing signified. It gives us no purchase on what God's goodness consists in; it merely labels the gap between human concept and divine reality. The analogical framework denies that the modus applies to God, and the res in its divine mode remains unknown, so the distinction leaves the content of 'good' as applied to God semantically underdetermined. The inference from introducing this distinction to providing resources to ground meaning therefore misses a step: classifying the structure of signification is not the same as determining its content. The premise treats a map of semantic relations as if it were the territory of semantic determination.
objection.premise_fails_because: Premise W7172336769.c010 fails because it conflates the formal classification of signification-structure with the substantive grounding of predicate-meaning, leaving the content of divine predicates unexplained.

objection.text: Consider a critic who argues that divine simplicity is incoherent because 'God is wise' and 'God is good' seem to predicate distinct attributes of one simple being. A defender responds using only Frege's sense/reference distinction: both sentences share the same reference (God himself) while differing in sense, much as 'the morning star is bright' and 'the evening star is bright' differ in sense but co-refer. This directly defuses the critic's worry that distinct predicates imply distinct properties in God. The response is complete without invoking analogy, proportionality, or any analogical framework. The critic's concern—that simplicity threatens coherent predication—is addressed purely by the Fregean diagnostic that sameness of reference is compatible with difference of sense. The premise claims Fregean diagnostics MUST be located within the doctrine of analogy to address such concerns, but this case shows the concerns are already addressable without that framework.
objection.premise_fails_because: Premise W7172336769.c009 fails because Fregean sense/reference diagnostics can independently resolve the critic's worry about distinct predicates implying distinct divine properties, making the 'must' claim false.

objection.text: In the practice of ritual chant, the phrase 'God is a lion' is both meaningful and liturgical, yet it violates the proposed constraints by equating the divine with a creature. The chant assumes a symbolic, not literal, mode where predications derive their force from communal usage and mythic resonance rather than semantic exclusivity. Here, the framework fails to account for how non-literal, culturally embedded language can carry theological weight without collapsing into absurdity or contradiction. The constraints, if applied, would dismiss valid devotional expressions merely for defying analytic neatness.
objection.premise_fails_because: W7172336769.c025 fails because it cannot accommodate meaningful non-literal predications like 'God is a lion' that function in religious practice.

objection.text: C003 claims that selected Fregean distinctions can defuse criticisms of divine simplicity. It smuggles in the assumption that the sense/reference distinction is a neutral, self-sufficient diagnostic: pick it out, apply it, and the criticism dissolves. But the Fregean distinction is not neutral. Its operation presupposes a determinate referent—God as a single, unified object to which multiple senses attach. The criticism of divine simplicity targets exactly that presupposition: if God is simple, it is unclear whether 'good' and 'wise' pick out one referent or whether the predicates carve God into incompatible slices. The Fregean move can only 'defuse' the criticism if it already grants the unity the critic denies. C009 and C010 confirm this: the Fregean distinctions cannot stand alone; they require embedding in the analogical framework (res significata / modus significandi) to secure a determinate referent. So the Fregean distinctions do not defuse the criticism; the analogical framework does, and the Fregean layer is merely a local diagnostic that functions only because the framework has already supplied the unity. C003 needs the Fregean distinctions to be self-sufficient but cannot have them, because their very operation presupposes the unified referent the criticism challenges.
objection.premise_fails_because: W7172336769.c003 fails because it treats the Fregean sense/reference distinction as a neutral, self-sufficient diagnostic, when in fact the distinction's operation presupposes a determinate unified referent—the very unity the criticism of divine simplicity denies—so the Fregean layer cannot defuse the criticism without already importing the answer the analogical framework must supply.

objection.text: Consider a theologian, Emma, who uses the Thomistic doctrine of analogy to interpret divine predicates. She believes that 'God is good' has a determinate meaning, but her interpretation relies on a complex web of metaphysical assumptions. In practice, Emma's community has varying understandings of 'good', leading to disagreements about God's nature. Despite the doctrine's constraints, the community's diverse perspectives on divine goodness persist, indicating that determinacy in theological language is not solely due to the doctrine's supplies.
objection.premise_fails_because: The hidden premise fails because it assumes that the determinacy supplied by the Thomistic doctrine of analogy is sufficient to answer worries about meaning, when in fact, the complexities of human interpretation and the persistence of diverse perspectives can undermine such determinacy.

objection.text: Consider the monk Ioannis of a remote monastery. He receives the uncreated divine energies in the Divine Liturgy, experiencing God’s love, wisdom, and power as living realities, not as merely semantic predicates. A philosopher using the analogical framework would say the rule “allow ‘God is good’ but exclude ‘God is a chair’” secures meaning. Yet Ioannis knows that calling God a chair is barred because the divine energies cannot be reduced to any created category, not because of a linguistic constraint. The same reason that permits “God is love” is the participation in the uncreated energy of love, which transcends any analogical semantic scheme. Thus the premise that analogical semantics alone supplies the principled exclusion fails to account for the essence‑energies distinction that truly governs divine predication.
objection.premise_fails_because: Premise W7172336769.c025 fails because analogical semantics alone cannot determine admissible divine predications; the true constraints come from the Eastern Orthodox distinction between God's essence and uncreated energies.

objection.text: A theologian believes that because analogy provides "sufficiently determinate content," the predicate "wise" and the predicate "good" correspond to distinct, determinate metaphysical specifications within the divine essence. Consequently, they treat God as a composite of these distinct specifications. This view forces a composition upon God, transforming the single, undivided Act of Being into a collection of distinct, determinate properties. By attempting to secure semantic determinacy, the theologian inadvertently destroys divine simplicity, which requires that God be absolutely without parts or multiplicity.
objection.premise_fails_because: W7172336769.c042 fails because "sufficiently determinate content" implies a multiplicity of distinct metaphysical specifications that would violate the principle of divine simplicity.

objection.text: A semantic theorist argues that for a predicate to carry determinate content, there must be a fixed and exhaustive relationship between the signifier and the signified. The doctrine of analogy, by design, preserves 'semantic openness,' meaning the relationship between the human term and the divine reality is intentionally left under-specified. objection.text: r3 concedes that the analogical framework excludes ill-formed predications (e.g., 'God is a chair') only conditional on a prior, independent classification of pure perfections. The argument needs r3 to function as a modest concession: the framework cannot settle every contested case ('God is mutable'), yet still supplies the determinacy that makes God-talk meaningful. But r3 severs the very link the conclusion requires. If even the exclusion of plainly incoherent predications depends on an external classification the framework does not itself generate, then the framework contributes no determinacy at all. The 'sufficiently determinate for meaning and practice' work attributed to the Thomistic doctrine in c005 is actually performed by the prior classification of creaturely features as pure perfections. r3 is treated as a limitation on scope (the framework cannot settle hard cases) while silently shifting the source of all determinacy outside the framework. The premise thus fails to support mp: it shows the framework is parasitic on an external input, not that it supplies principled constraints while leaving residual openness.
